## Part 2 — Ask, look, decide

### Step 1: the per-sample numbers

Suggested request: *In step 1 of my notebook, make one data frame with a row
for every sample in each count table, species and genes, and a `table` column
saying which. Columns: library size, number of features detected, fraction of
zeros, the share held by the largest feature, Shannon diversity, and the
effective number of features.*

```{r step1-per-sample-stats}
# Turn a count table (features in rows, samples in columns)
# into one row per sample.
per_sample_stats <- function(counts) {
  mat <- as.matrix(counts[-1])   # drop the feature-id column, keep the counts
  lib_size <- colSums(mat)       # total reads per sample
  # each cell as a fraction of its sample's total
  p <- sweep(mat, 2, lib_size, "/")
  # natural log Shannon; zero cells contribute 0
  shannon <- -colSums(p * log(p), na.rm = TRUE)
  n_detected <- colSums(mat > 0)
  tibble::tibble(
    sample_id          = colnames(mat),
    library_size       = lib_size,
    features_detected  = n_detected,
    fraction_zeros     = 1 - n_detected / nrow(mat),
    largest_share      = apply(p, 2, max),
    shannon            = shannon,
    # number of equally common features with the same Shannon
    effective_features = exp(shannon)
  )
}

per_sample <- bind_rows(
  per_sample_stats(species) |> mutate(table = "species"),
  per_sample_stats(genes)   |> mutate(table = "genes")
)
per_sample
```


### Step 2: a short report

Suggested request: *Under that data frame, add a summary table with the median,
smallest and largest value of every column, separately for each table. Then
write three sentences about anything unusual.*

```{r step2-summary}
# Median, smallest and largest of every numeric column, one block per table.
# The pivots turn the wide summary into a long table that is easy to read:
# one row per column, with its median, min and max.
per_sample |>
  group_by(table) |>
  summarise(across(where(is.numeric),
                   list(median = median, min = min, max = max)),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_longer(-table, names_to = c("column", "stat"),
               names_pattern = "(.*)_(min|max|median)") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = stat, values_from = value) |>
  relocate(column, median, min, max)
```

Three things in this table that stand out:

1. The two tables live at completely different scales: the gene table's median
   library size is about 12 million reads against about 28,700 for species. The
   RNA-seq sequencing was roughly a thousand times deeper, so "big library"
   means different things in each table.
2. Some species samples are nearly monocultures: the largest feature can hold
   up to 99.9% of reads and the effective number drops to 1.01, meaning one
   species in practice. The smallest libraries are not the cause — the 438-read
   sample has a healthy effective number of 9.8 — instead it is the week-34
   samples, where one species takes over.
3. Even the richest gene sample detects 14,200 of 14,226 genes, so a handful of
   genes are essentially never expressed in any sample — a low ceiling the
   species table does not have, where the best sample sees only 70 of 220.

- Which medians were furthest from your Part 1 answers?
  - *Your answer:*Genes detected (guessed 10,500, real about 14,100), then gene effective number (guessed 500, real about 1,050).
- Did Pi mention the 438-read sample? Did it claim anything you cannot find in the table?
  - *Your answer:*Yes, in sentence 2, where it called the sample “healthy”. It also made three claims the data contradicts or can’t support:
Genes “never expressed in any sample”: I checked, and 0 genes are empty in every sample.
“Roughly a thousand times deeper”: the real ratio is about 425×.
“It is the week-34 samples”: week 24 has 41 of the 93 and week 34 has 39.

### Step 3: one number, four plots

Suggested request: *Plot the library size of every sample four ways: a
histogram, the same histogram on a log scale, the samples ranked from smallest
to largest, and library size by visit. Use both tables.*

```{r step3-library-size}
# `per_sample` already has library_size for both tables (Step 1).
# Join on the metadata to get each sample's visit, then make the four plots.
lib_size <- per_sample |>
  left_join(metadata |> select(sample_id, time_point), by = "sample_id")

# 1. Histogram, raw scale.
#    Problem: the gene libraries are ~1000x deeper than the species ones, so on
#    this scale every species sample piles into one bar at the far left and the
#    genes fill a narrow sliver at the far right.
ggplot(lib_size, aes(x = library_size, fill = table)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  # separate panels, each with its own x axis
  facet_wrap(~ table, scales = "free") +
  labs(title = "Library size, raw counts",
       x = "Reads per sample", y = "Samples") +
  theme_minimal()

# 2. Same histogram on a log scale.
#    log10 squashes big numbers much more than small ones, so samples a
#    thousand-fold apart can sit on the same axis and the shape of each
#    distribution becomes visible.
ggplot(lib_size, aes(x = library_size, fill = table)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  # free_x: each table spans its own range
  facet_wrap(~ table, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(title = "Library size, log scale",
       x = "Reads per sample (log10)", y = "Samples") +
  theme_minimal()

# 3. Samples ranked from smallest to largest.
#    Each dot is one sample. This makes single odd samples stand out: a very
#    low dot at the left end, gaps in the staircase, or a long flat tail.
#    Sort by library size first, then rank = 1, 2, 3, ... within each table.
ranked <- lib_size |>
  group_by(table) |>
  arrange(library_size, .by_group = TRUE) |>
  mutate(rank = row_number()) |>
  ungroup()

ggplot(ranked, aes(x = rank, y = library_size, colour = table)) +
  geom_point(size = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ table, scales = "free") +
  labs(title = "Samples ranked by library size",
       x = "Rank (1 = smallest library)", y = "Reads per sample") +
  theme_minimal()

# 4. Library size by visit.
#    A boxplot per visit shows whether one visit was sequenced more deeply than
#    another. Points are jittered (nudged sideways) so overlapping samples show.
ggplot(lib_size, aes(x = time_point, y = library_size, fill = time_point)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, size = 0.5, alpha = 0.4) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  facet_wrap(~ table, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Library size by visit",
       x = "Visit", y = "Reads per sample (log10)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

- Which view makes the 438-read sample obvious, and which hides it? Which would you put in a paper?
  - *Your answer:* The **rank plot** makes it obvious: the 438-read sample is the
    dot sitting alone at the bottom-left, detached from the rest of the
    staircase, and it is the only view that also tells me *which* sample it is.
    The log histogram shows it too, as a tiny isolated bar at the far left, but
    only tells me *a* shallow sample exists, not which one. The **raw
    histogram** hides it: everything below ~4,000 reads is crammed into one
    bar at the left edge, and on a raw axis the 65-fold gap between 438 and
    28,700 looks like nothing. The by-visit boxplot half-hides it as one
    anonymous dot below the week-18 whisker.
    For a paper I would use the **log-scale histogram** — it shows the whole
    distribution honestly without letting one extreme sample stretch the axis,
    and log library-size histograms are a standard methods figure in
    sequencing papers; if justifying a minimum-library-size cutoff, I would
    add the rank plot as a supplementary figure. The **raw histogram** and the
    **by-visit boxplot** are for my eyes only: the raw one is a first sanity
    check that the tables live at different scales, and the by-visit one
    answers "was one visit sequenced more shallowly?" (no — the medians match),
    after which it has done its job. Key contrast: the log histogram shows me
    the shallow samples exist; the rank plot tells me who they are.

### Step 4: features detected against library size

From here on, write your own requests. Ask for the plot and the Spearman
correlation for each table, then ask how many extra genes the correlation
amounts to between the shallowest and the deepest samples.

```{r step4-detected-vs-size}
# Scatter: features detected (y) against library size (x), one panel per table.
# Spearman correlation measures whether more reads -> more features detected,
# without assuming a straight-line relationship.
ggplot(per_sample, aes(x = library_size, y = features_detected, colour = table)) +
  geom_point(size = 1, alpha = 0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ table, scales = "free") +
  labs(title = "Features detected against library size",
       x = "Reads per sample", y = "Features detected") +
  theme_minimal()

# The Spearman correlation for each table.
per_sample |>
  group_by(table) |>
  summarise(spearman = cor(library_size, features_detected,
                           method = "spearman"),
            shallowest = min(library_size),
            deepest = max(library_size),
            .groups = "drop")

# How many extra features between the shallowest and deepest sample?
# Pick out the two extreme samples from each table and compare them.
per_sample |>
  group_by(table) |>
  filter(library_size == min(library_size) |
         library_size == max(library_size)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  select(table, sample_id, library_size, features_detected) |>
  arrange(table, library_size)

# Same idea as a straight line: on average, how many extra features does each
# extra million reads buy? (The Spearman does not need this, but it turns the
# correlation into a number you can reason with.)
per_sample |>
  group_by(table) |>
  summarise(extra_per_million = coef(lm(features_detected ~ library_size))[2] * 1e6,
            .groups = "drop")
```

- How many extra genes, out of 14,226? Does the plot agree with Pi?
  - *Your answer:* The Spearman correlation for genes is 0.50 — moderate, not
    the "strong" I was told to expect — and for species it is 0.06, essentially
    nothing. Between the shallowest gene sample (P086_week_24, 6.0 million
    reads, 13,830 genes) and the deepest (P053_week_34, 28.8 million reads,
    14,142 genes) the difference is only **312 extra genes**, about 2% of the
    14,226. The plot agrees: the rightmost gene dot sits at ~14,140 and the
    shallowest at ~13,830, and the whole cloud rises only ~500 genes across
    the full depth range while the vertical spread at any one depth is far
    larger. The line fit puts it at ~11 extra genes per million reads; 22.8
    million extra reads times 11 ≈ 250, close to the observed 312. So a
    visible upward trend can still be a small effect — even the shallowest
    sample already sees 97% of all genes. In the species panel depth matters
    even less: the 438-read sample detects 20 species and the deepest (155,686
    reads) only 37, because most species are common enough to appear in almost
    every sample. That is why the raw histogram's axis made the species table
    look so stretched: the outliers matter for the eye, not for detection.

### Step 5: which samples to drop

Ask Pi to suggest a minimum library size and explain it. Then ask how many
samples cutoffs of 1,000, 5,000, 10,000 and 20,000 reads would drop, and from
which visits and outcomes.

```{r step5-cutoffs}
# `per_sample` has library_size for both tables; join on the metadata for
# visit and outcome, then count who each cutoff would drop.
lib_meta <- per_sample |>
  left_join(metadata |> select(sample_id, time_point, outcome),
            by = "sample_id")

species_meta <- lib_meta |> filter(table == "species")

# For one cutoff: total dropped, dropped by visit, dropped by outcome,
# and group sizes that survive. Returns a little data frame.
who_dropped <- function(cut) {
  drop <- species_meta |> filter(library_size < cut)
  kept <- species_meta |> filter(library_size >= cut)
  bind_rows(
    tibble(what = "dropped, total", group = "all samples", n = nrow(drop)),
    drop |> count(time_point) |>
      transmute(what = "dropped, visit", group = time_point, n),
    drop |> count(outcome) |>
      transmute(what = "dropped, outcome", group = outcome, n),
    kept |> count(outcome) |>
      transmute(what = "kept, outcome", group = outcome, n)
  )
}

# Apply it to each cutoff and put the cutoffs side by side.
cutoff_table <- bind_rows(
  who_dropped(1000)   |> mutate(cutoff = 1000),
  who_dropped(5000)   |> mutate(cutoff = 5000),
  who_dropped(10000)  |> mutate(cutoff = 10000),
  who_dropped(20000)  |> mutate(cutoff = 20000)
)

cutoff_table |>
  select(cutoff, what, group, n) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = cutoff, values_from = n,
              names_prefix = "< ")

# the samples the 1,000 cutoff would drop, so we can see them individually
species_meta |> filter(library_size < 1000)
```

*The cutoff I chose, and why:* I would use **1,000 reads minimum for the
species table**. The 438-read sample is an order of magnitude below the next
smallest (2,489) and about 65-fold below the median (~28,700); with 438 reads
a sample cannot represent a community of 220 species, so its species counts
and its diversities are noise no matter how they look. The cutoff costs
almost nothing: one sample out of 471, a term week-18 sample, so no group
loses a disproportionate share. The table shows why I stop there: 5,000 reads
only adds two more shallow week-18 samples (both with sensible feature
counts), while 20,000 would delete 96 samples — 20% of the dataset, 56 of
them from week 18 — buying precision we do not need. Losing samples evenly
across visits and outcomes costs little; cutting 20% of one visit would bias
any visit comparison. A stricter rule (5,000) would also be defensible if a
reviewer expected it, because it drops only 3 samples and keeps every group
well stocked; what I would not do is justify 20,000, which sacrifices even
sampling for a cutoff most of the data never needed.
